Deep dive · world action models · 24 November 2026

Why WAMs?

Most robot brains look and react. A world action model looks, imagines the next second, and then moves to make that imagined second happen. We ran one in a simulated kitchen to see what that is like from the inside, and to find out whether the imagining is worth what it costs.

Press Play. What it pictured and what then happened match well, and the robot finishes the task. What it costs is time: with the released settings, on our GPU, it spent 3.4 seconds thinking for every 0.8 seconds of moving.

So is the imagining worth it? We will follow one second of this robot's thinking, with every tensor it builds on the way; see how it learned to think like that; and then weigh the cost. Under each step are two folds: the maths and code, and a drawing from first principles. You can skip both.

  1. 1One second inside its head
  2. 2How it learned that
  3. 3Is the imagining worth it?
  4. 4Paper vs release, and how we checked

1One second inside its head

The robot is LingBot-VA, an open model from Robbyant (Ant Group), running through LeRobot's own code. The world is LIBERO: a simulated kitchen with one robot arm, a camera across the table, a camera on the wrist, and 20 moves a second. The task is "put both moka pots on the stove". It managed it in 361 moves and 23 plans. The first plan covers 12 moves and every later one 16, so plan 3 starts at move 28. We freeze it there and watch. (Timings and success rates come from a separate run over all 10 LIBERO-Long tasks: 10 of 10 solved.)

It looks and reads

Each camera hands over one picture, 128 pixels on a side, and every pixel is three numbers for red, green and blue. So what the robot sees at one moment is a block of numbers with shape [2, 3, 128, 128]: 2 cameras, 3 colours, 128 rows, 128 columns. That is 98,304 numbers, and a fresh block arrives with every move. It is never told where its own joints are; the moves it has already made stand in for that.

The words take their own path. A frozen text encoder, UMT5-XXL, turns the sentence into 512 slots of 4096 numbers; a short sentence fills a few and the rest are blanks. A small two-layer network maps each slot to 3072, the model's width: [512, 4096] → [512, 3072]. Every layer then reads the words through cross-attention: each picture token asks a question \(q\) and gets back a weighted mix of the word slots,

\[ \text{cross-attention}(q) = \text{softmax}\!\Big(\frac{q\,K_{\text{words}}^\top}{\sqrt{128}}\Big)\,V_{\text{words}} \]

where \(K_{\text{words}}\) and \(V_{\text{words}}\) are the slots turned into keys (what each slot is about) and values (what it says), 128 is the size of one attention head, and the softmax turns the 512 scores into weights that add up to 1.

text_encoder_device: str = "cpu"   # configuration_lingbot_va.py: "frees ~11 GB VRAM (it runs once per episode)"
max_sequence_length: int = 512     # the 512 word slots
text_hidden_states = self.condition_embedder.text_embedder(input_dict["text_emb"])  # utils.py:1064, 4096 -> 3072

The checkpoint's inputs are the two camera images only (obs_cam_keys); LIBERO also offers the arm's joint state, and this model does not use it. The paper's reason: in its own robot data the moves are absolute hand poses, so the history of moves already says where the arm is.

Check yourself. Our two-arm SO-101 has three cameras. At 128 × 128 each, what is the shape of one moment? Answer: [3, 3, 128, 128], 147,456 numbers.

First principleswords to numbers

Check yourself. If all 512 slots scored the same, what share would the 9 real ones get? Answer: 9/512 = 1.8%.

It shrinks what it sees

The heart of this model is a transformer, and a transformer compares every piece of its input with every other piece. Twice the pieces is four times the work. Feeding it raw pixels would mean millions of pieces, so first the pictures go through a squeezer: the VAE of Wan2.2, the video generator this model grew from (part 2). A VAE is a network trained on huge amounts of video to shrink it and blow it back up. It stays frozen: we never retrain it, so the shrunk version of a scene means the same thing throughout training and the model always aims at a fixed target.

The squeezer takes 4 moves' worth of pictures at once and returns one small grid: 8 by 16 spots (the two cameras side by side), with 48 numbers at each spot. We call that grid a latent frame; one latent frame stands for 4 camera frames. Then the grid is cut into 2 × 2 patches, and each patch becomes one token, the unit the transformer works with:

\[ \tfrac{8 \times 16}{2 \times 2} = 32 \text{ tokens}, \qquad 48 \times 2 \times 2 = 192 \text{ numbers each} \xrightarrow{\;\times W\;} 3072 \]

\(W\) is one learned 192 × 3072 matrix. For one latent frame: [2, 3, 4, 128, 128] → [48, 8, 16] → [32, 192] → [32, 3072]. The picture in the bottom left shows what survives: decoded back, the frame keeps its layout and loses its fine texture. Everything the robot imagines lives at that blurry resolution.

Go deepershapes and code
  1. The VAE gives a mean \(\mu\) and a spread for each spot; the code keeps \(\mu\). Its rhythm is causal, "1 + 4k": the first frame of an episode becomes one latent frame on its own, then every 4 new frames become one more. While acting, frames stream in (1, then 12, then 16 per plan) and none are lost.
  2. Each of the 48 channels is shifted and scaled with the VAE's stored statistics, \(z_c = (\mu_c - m_c)/s_c\), so every channel has about zero mean and unit spread, like the static of the next step.
  3. Compression: \(4 \times 2 \times 3 \times 128 \times 128 = 393{,}216\) numbers become \(48 \times 8 \times 16 = 6{,}144\), 64 times fewer.
  4. A plan is 4 latent frames, so 128 frame tokens; with its 16 move tokens, the transformer handles 144 new tokens per plan.
mu, _logvar = torch.chunk(enc_out, 2, dim=1)               # modeling_lingbot_va.py:547, keep the mean
video_latent = torch.cat(mu_norm.split(1, dim=0), dim=-1)  # :575, cameras side by side
latent_hidden_states = rearrange(input_dict["noisy_latents"],
    "b c (f p1) (h p2) (w p3) -> b (f h w) (c p1 p2 p3)", p1=1, p2=2, p3=2)
latent_hidden_states = self.patch_embedding_mlp(latent_hidden_states)   # utils.py:1063, 192 -> 3072

Check yourself. With three cameras side by side, how many tokens per latent frame? Answer: the grid is 8 × 24, so (8/2)(24/2) = 48 tokens, 192 per plan.

First principlesinside the VAE

Check yourself. Which stage would you change to keep twice as many latent frames? Answer: drop one time convolution (stage 1 or 2).

It imagines the next second

It is going to imagine the next 4 latent frames, which is the next 16 moves. It cannot just output the next frame. The future is not one thing: the arm could swing left or right of the pot. A network trained to output the next frame, scored by squared error, learns the average of all the futures it has seen, and the average of "left" and "right" is an arm swinging through the middle of the pot.

So instead it starts from pure static, random numbers in the shape of 4 latent frames, [48, 4, 8, 16], and cleans the static up a little at a time. The method is called flow matching. In training, take a real future \(x\) and some static \(\varepsilon\), and mix them:

\[ x_\sigma = (1 - \sigma)\,x + \sigma\,\varepsilon \]

\(\sigma\) is how much static is left: at \(\sigma = 0\) it is the real future, at \(\sigma = 1\) it is all static. As \(\sigma\) grows from 0 to 1, \(x_\sigma\) slides in a straight line from the future to the static, always in the direction \(\varepsilon - x\). The network \(v\) is shown \(x_\sigma\) and asked for that direction. Many lines pass through any one point, and squared error is smallest at their mean, so \(v\) learns the average direction through each point. To imagine, it walks the line the other way, from static toward a future, in small clean-up steps:

\[ x \;\leftarrow\; x + v(x, \sigma)\,(\sigma_{\text{next}} - \sigma) \]

Because \(\sigma_{\text{next}}\) is smaller than \(\sigma\), each clean-up step removes a slice of static. Here is the whole idea in one dimension, with two possible futures:

clean-up steps

A toy, not the robot: each line is one walk from static (left) toward two possible futures at −1.5 and +1.2 (right), using the exact best direction, which can be worked out for a toy this small.

With 1 clean-up step every walk lands on the average of the two futures: the blurry middle. With more steps, each walk starts toward the middle and then commits. Early on a point could still belong to either future, so the best direction points between them; as it moves, its position gives away which future it is heading for, and the best direction turns toward that one. That is why a sampler built from averages still ends on one sharp future.

The robot takes 20 clean-up steps, bunched up at the noisy end. Their spacing comes from one formula, a warp of evenly spaced values:

\[ \sigma' = \frac{5\,\sigma}{1 + 4\,\sigma} \qquad \text{so } 0.95 \mapsto 0.99,\;\; 0.5 \mapsto 0.83 \]

Most steps happen while the picture is still mostly static, which is where the big decisions get made: where the arm goes, where the pot ends up. Each clean-up step also runs the network twice, once with the instruction and once with an empty one, and pushes extra hard in the direction the words add:

\[ v = v_{\text{empty}} + 5\,(v_{\text{words}} - v_{\text{empty}}) \]

The difference in brackets is the part of the direction that comes from "moka pots" rather than from "some kitchen". Multiplying it by 5 makes the imagination follow the words closely, and it doubles the work. This is called guidance.

Go deeperwhy it works, and the code
  1. Training minimises \(\mathbb E\,\| v(x_\sigma, \sigma) - (\varepsilon - x)\|^2\). Fix \(\sigma\) and a point: many lines pass through it, and a squared error is smallest at the mean, so the best network is \(v^*(x_\sigma, \sigma) = \mathbb E[\varepsilon - x \mid x_\sigma]\), the average direction of the lines through that point.
  2. Moving every point along \(v^*\) carries the whole cloud of static onto the whole cloud of real futures (the density obeys the continuity equation \(\partial_\sigma p + \nabla\cdot(p\,v^*) = 0\)), so a fresh sample of static ends as a fresh, sharp future, not as the mean.
  3. At \(\sigma = 1\) the point is pure static and says nothing about the future, so \(v^* = x_\sigma - \mathbb E[x]\), and one step to \(\sigma = 0\) lands everyone on \(\mathbb E[x]\): the blur. In the toy that is \(0.45(-1.5) + 0.55(1.2) = -0.015\).
  4. The paper writes the same line with the clock reversed, \(s = 1 - \sigma\), and the direction \(x - \varepsilon\).

Each dot is one clean-up step from the code's own scheduler; the shading is where training practises. Frames spend 17 of 20 steps noisier than halfway; moves spend 34 of 50 within 10% of clean. Training draws one \(\sigma\) per latent frame, separately for frames and moves, warped the same way, so its median is the warp of 0.5: 0.833 for frames, 0.048 for moves.

sample = (1 - sigma) * original_samples + sigma * noise            # utils.py:277, the mix
target = noise - sample                                            # utils.py:281, the direction
prev_sample = sample + model_output * (sigma_ - sigma)             # utils.py:266, one clean-up step
self.sigmas = self.shift * self.sigmas / (1 + (self.shift - 1) * self.sigmas)  # utils.py:239, the warp
video_noise_pred = video_noise_pred[1:] + cfg.guidance_scale * (   # modeling_lingbot_va.py:795, guidance
    video_noise_pred[:1] - video_noise_pred[1:])

Check yourself. In the toy, a point at \(x = 2\) with \(\sigma = 1\) takes one clean-up step to \(\sigma = 0.5\). Where does it land? Answer: \(2 + (2 - (-0.015))(0.5 - 1) = 0.9925\): halfway to the blur, on neither future.

Check yourself. Columns 3 and 4 show two different cameras. How far apart does attention think they are? Answer: one column, like any neighbours.

It reads off its moves

Next it needs the moves: 16 of them, each 7 numbers (shift the hand in x, y and z; turn it three ways; open or close the gripper), so [16, 7] (inside the model a move has 30 slots, one layout for every robot; LIBERO uses 7). LIBERO reads each number, between −1 and 1, as a fraction of the most the hand may change in one move: 5 cm of position, half a radian of angle. So the first move's Δx of 0.60 asks for about 3 cm forward. It uses the same clean-up trick, in 50 steps bunched at the clean end (\(\sigma' = 0.05\sigma / (1 - 0.95\sigma)\)), because a move is a handful of numbers where a millimetre matters, and the work is in the final polish.

The important part is what the moves get to look at. After the 20th clean-up step of the frames, one extra pass writes the imagined frames into the model's memory (more on memory below). The move tokens then run through the same layers and attend to everything in memory, imagined frames included. Deciding what to do from a picture of now is hard; deciding what to do when you also have a picture of where things should be a moment later is close to arithmetic: find the move that gets from here to there. Roboticists call that inverse dynamics. In symbols, the robot makes two draws, with \(\hat z_{\text{next}}\) the imagined latent frames:

\[ \underbrace{\hat z_{\text{next}} \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \text{past frames, past moves, words})}_{\text{imagine}} \qquad \underbrace{\text{moves} \sim p(\,\cdot \mid \hat z_{\text{next}}, \text{past}, \text{words})}_{\text{read the moves}} \]

Read the grid above row by row and it tells the same story as the imagined frames: the hand moves forward while slowing down, sinks, rotates, and keeps the gripper open. It is reaching down for the pot. The imagined frames do not depend on the moves: they are a plan of what should happen, not a forecast of what a move would cause.

That is the difference from a VLA. A VLA goes straight from now to moves, so it has to average over every future it can't see: \(p(\text{moves} \mid \text{now}) = \int p(\text{future} \mid \text{now})\, p(\text{moves} \mid \text{now}, \text{future})\, d\,\text{future}\). LingBot-VA replaces the average with one imagined future.

Go deeperone network, two jobs

Frames and moves go through one stack of 30 layers, 5.09 billion parameters; only 1.75% of them belong to moves alone. A frame token enters through a 192 → 3072 matrix and a move through a 30 → 3072 one: inside the model a move is 30 numbers, so one layout fits every robot (per arm a 7-number hand pose, up to 7 joints and the gripper, times 2 arms; LIBERO fills 7). A plan's 16 moves are stored as [30, 4, 4]: 30 numbers, 4 latent frames, 4 moves each. Each token also carries a time: frames at whole numbers, the 4 moves between frames 0 and 1 at 0.2, 0.4, 0.6 and 0.8. Attention sees time through rotary position encoding: part of each 128-number attention head is rotated by an angle proportional to the time, so a question and a key compare only by how far apart they are.

latent_hidden_states = self.action_embedder(latent_hidden_states)       # utils.py:1054, a move: 30 -> 3072
ff_offset = (torch.ones([h]).cumsum(0) / (h + 1)).view(1, -1, 1)       # utils.py:89, times 1/5 .. 4/5
if is_first:
    a = a[:, :, 1:]      # modeling_lingbot_va.py:472, the first plan drops frame 0: 12 moves, then 16

Check yourself. How many moves do the first three plans cover? Answer: 12 + 16 + 16 = 44. The first plan is shorter because its first latent frame is the real starting picture.

First principlesstatic to motor command

Check yourself. The model outputs 0 for Δx. Does the hand stay still? Answer: no, 0 maps to 0.12: about 6 mm forward.

It moves, then checks

The arm plays all 16 moves without looking. Then the robot does the thing that keeps it honest: it deletes what it imagined and writes what the cameras actually saw, and the moves it made, into its memory. The next plan starts from reality.

The memory is the transformer's KV cache: every processed token leaves a key and a value in each of the 30 layers, and new tokens attend to them just as they attend to the words. Old plans never attend to new ones, so their keys and values never change and are stored, not recomputed. There is room for 15 plans, 2,160 tokens, about 12 seconds. Imagining needs room too, so once the memory is full the oldest plan is pushed out and the robot imagines from the last 14.

Go deeperwhat it costs

Size: 2 (keys and values) × 2 (the guidance pair) × 2,160 tokens × 3,072 numbers × 2 bytes × 30 layers = 1.59 GB. Per plan the model computes 144 new tokens against at most 2,160 keys, the size of the memory, instead of re-reading the whole history. Per plan it runs the network 74 times: 21 frame passes (20 clean-up steps plus the one that writes the imagined frames into memory) and 51 move passes (50 + 1), each as a pair for guidance, plus 2 passes that write reality back (72 on the first plan).

self.transformer.clear_pred_cache("pos")                 # modeling_lingbot_va.py:721, forget the imagination
latent_model_input = self._encode_frames(obs_buffer)     # squeeze what really happened
self.transformer(..., update_cache=2, action_mode=False) # real frames into memory, kept
self.transformer(..., update_cache=2, action_mode=True)  # the moves it made, kept

Check yourself. Which moves go back into memory: the ones the arm executed, or the ones the model planned? Answer: in LeRobot, the planned ones (self._executed_actions = actions). They are the same as long as the arm does exactly what it is told.

First principlesthe memory, slot by slot

Check yourself. Why does the 21st frame pass keep its tokens? Answer: so the move passes can read the imagined frames.

That is the loop: look, shrink, imagine, read the moves, move, check. It ran 23 times to put both pots on the stove. Here it is on one page, with the shape of every tensor:

2How it learned that

The 5-billion-parameter network did not start from nothing. It started as Wan2.2, a video generator trained on a large amount of video from the web, so before it ever saw a robot it already had a rough sense of how scenes move. Robbyant then trained it on about 16,000 hours of robots doing tasks, with the moves recorded alongside the video, and finally on LIBERO itself, 50 recordings per task. The middle stage matters: in the paper, skipping it and starting straight from Wan2.2 gives 80.6% success on a two-arm benchmark instead of 92.9%. So more robot video with moves helps a lot. Whether video helps beyond that is the question of part 3.

Each training stage uses the same trick. Lay each recording out twice, side by side. One copy is exactly as recorded. The other is buried in static, a random amount per latent frame. The network's job is to clean up the buried copy, frames and moves both, while looking at the clean one. It is the same trick that trains a language model on a whole sentence in one go. Two copies are needed because a noisy frame is no use as context for the frames after it: they read the clean copy.

What makes it work is a rule about who may look at what. The noisy frames of a plan may look only at the real past, so they learn to picture what comes next. The noisy moves of a plan may look at the real past and at the real frames of their own plan, so they learn the move that produces those frames. Both are scored the same way, by how far the network's direction is from the true one:

\[ \mathcal{L} = \big\| v(x_\sigma) - (\varepsilon - x) \big\|^2_{\text{frames}} + \big\| v(a_\sigma) - (\varepsilon - a) \big\|^2_{\text{moves}} \]

(The code also weights each term by its noise level; the training fold draws the weights.)

Here is the gap. When the robot acts, the real next frames do not exist yet, so it hands its moves the imagined frames instead. Training on real frames and acting on imagined ones is the bet this whole design makes, and as far as we can find, nobody has measured what it costs. To soften the switch, half the time in training the clean past is itself smudged with static, so the network gets used to reading imperfect pictures.

Go deeperthe full rule
Tap a row: what may this token read?

Computed by running the code's own mask on a small example: 4 latent frames of 1 token each, 2 moves per frame, 2 frames per plan (V = frames, A = moves, n = noisy, c = clean). The rule in one line: give the frames of plan \(k\) the number \(2k\) and its moves \(2k + 1\); clean reads clean up to its own number; noisy reads clean with a smaller number; noisy reads noisy only with the same number. Noisy moves of plan \(k\) (\(2k+1\)) can therefore read the clean frames of plan \(k\) (\(2k\)), which is the inverse-dynamics rule. The smudging of the past goes up to 83% static in the code, against at most 50% in the paper.

mask_list.append(and_masks(clean2clean_mask, block_causal_mask))               # utils.py:466, clean reads clean, up to its own number
mask_list.append(and_masks(noise2clean_mask, block_causal_mask_exclude_self))  # noisy reads clean, strictly smaller number
mask_list.append(and_masks(noise2noise_mask, block_self_mask))                 # noisy reads noisy, same number

Check yourself. What clean context do the noisy frames of the very first plan get? Answer: none. When acting, the first plan is instead anchored by pinning its first latent frame to the real starting picture at every clean-up step.

3Is the imagining worth it?

First, the bill. Here is where one plan's time went in our run:

And part of that is wasted. Each move pass also runs an empty-prompt copy for guidance, but move guidance is 1, which means no push, so that copy is computed and thrown away.

That bill is for the released settings. The paper's own are leaner: 3 clean-up steps for the frames, stopping before the picture is finished, and 10 for the moves. Stopping early works, which hints that the moves need the layout, not the detail. The paper also plans the next chunk while the arm is still moving. Neither is in the release we ran.

Planning while moving is harder than it looks. While a plan runs, the newest real picture is already old, and planning from the model's own imagined outcome is exactly the drift that writing reality into memory avoids: in the paper, success on three-stage tasks falls from 93.2% to 32.9%. The fix is a forward model: from the latest real frame and the moves now running, imagine what those moves will produce, then plan from that. Unlike the plan, this is a true "what happens if I do this" forecast.

So could you keep what video teaches and skip the imagining altogether when acting? A group tested exactly that (Fast-WAM, March 2026). They built four versions of one model on the same data: no video in training; Fast-WAM, video in training but never imagined when acting; imagine then act, a video model imagines and a separate model reads the moves off it; and joint denoising, one network cleans up frames and moves together. LingBot-VA, one network that imagines and then reads the moves, sits between the last two.

Take video out of training and success drops 8 points on RoboTwin, a two-arm benchmark. Keep video in training but skip imagining when acting, and success moves by about a point either way, at a quarter to a third of the delay. In their version the moves never look at imagined frames at all, so whatever video teaches has to reach the moves through the layers the two share. If that holds up, the value of video is in what it teaches, and the pictures at run time are optional. Two cautions: one group built all four versions, and one independent robustness study found the imagining models weaker when the camera is moved (45.6% success for π0.5, a model without video, against 28.9% for LingBot-VA).

The companies split along the same line. The only one with a named paying customer, Dyna (its robots fold napkins at Din Tai Fung), trains on a million hours of human video and publishes a policy that does not imagine when it acts. NVIDIA, Dream Labs and Robbyant imagine at run time and have no named deployments yet. Most of these numbers are the companies' own.

Imagining is getting cheaper, though. Robbyant's second version reports 142 ms per plan, down from 927 ms for the same model before its speed-ups: 2 clean-up steps (it puts the first version at 5 and 10; that paper itself says 3 and 10), 8-bit arithmetic, leaner memory handling (the hardware is not stated). It also swaps the pixel squeezer for one trained to keep meaning, which on its own lifts a 1.3-billion-parameter test model from 78.0% to 86.6% on RoboTwin. If those hold, the trade changes.

Our take: learning to predict video is worth it; imagining while acting has not yet earned its cost. For our two-arm SO-101 the cheap experiment is to train with video and act without it. And the most useful thing we could do for everyone is measure the bet from part 2: how much worse the moves get when they read imagined frames instead of real ones.

4Paper vs release

Paper vs releasefive differences
  • The release has one shared stack of layers, where the paper describes two networks side by side; 20 frame and 50 move clean-up steps, not 3 and 10; no plan-while-moving mode; smudging of the past up to 83% static, not 50%; and the move encoder and decoder are single matrices, not small networks.
  • The paper's text against its own tables: "10.3% better with 10 demonstrations" is the 5-demonstration gap (10 gives 7.5); "best on all six real tasks" fails for folding clothes (48.8 vs 62.9); "92.0% on RoboTwin" matches neither 92.9 nor 91.6.
  • Possible bugs in LeRobot's training path (read in the code, not run): moves enter training un-normalised; the instruction is never dropped, so the empty-prompt branch that guidance needs is never trained by fine-tuning; in training, 3 of every 16 frames are dropped by the squeezer's 1 + 4k rhythm.
How this page was checkedevery number, recomputed

A script recomputes every number on the page and refuses to build it if one is off. Where the page says how the code behaves, the script runs LeRobot's own code: the scheduler, the training mask, the time positions, the network built from its config. The run's numbers come from our own job on Explorer (one A100, LeRobot's evaluation code, 10 LIBERO-Long tasks, all 10 solved).
